query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Coating tungsten (W) particles with a thin nickel (Ni) layer before spark plasma sintering improves copper (Cu) wetting at the W–Cu interface, thereby reducing void formation and phase separation while preserving mechanical durability under irradiation compared to a baseline produced from uncoated W particles.
generation.material_initial_state: A composite fabricated from W particles (or connected W regions) embedded in a Cu matrix via spark plasma sintering, where conventional processing leads to voids and phase separation.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin Ni interfacial coating to the W particles prior to their incorporation into the Cu matrix, then process the composite by spark plasma sintering under controlled temperatures and pressures.
generation.conditions: Processing: Ni-coated W particles are mixed with Cu powder and sintered using spark plasma sintering with a controlled temperature profile (keeping Cu molten but below its boiling point) and an applied pressure to ensure densification. Service: The resulting composite is evaluated under irradiation conditions that simulate fusion reactor joint environments. Controlled variables include sintering temperature, pressure, and dwell time. Evaluation includes thermal transport and mechanical robustness under irradiation.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced interfacial bonding between W and Cu provided by the Ni layer, which promotes improved wetting and densification while reducing void formation.
generation.mechanism: The thin Ni coating acts as a wetting promoter and diffusional bridge at the W–Cu interface, lowering the interfacial energy barrier during sintering. This improves Cu infiltration and adhesion to the W particles, which minimizes the formation of voids and suppresses phase separation, leading to a more uniform composite with robust thermal and mechanical characteristics under irradiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Primary measured property: Thermal conductivity. The hypothesis predicts that Ni-coated W–Cu composites will exhibit improved thermal transport (and enhanced mechanical durability) relative to composites fabricated from uncoated W particles.
generation.baseline: A spark plasma sintered W–Cu composite made using uncoated W particles, which typically exhibits voids and phase separation that impair thermal transport.
generation.boundary: Applicable to composites processed via spark plasma sintering under conditions that maintain Cu in a molten state (but below its boiling point) and tested under irradiation environments relevant to fusion reactor joints.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the improvements in thermal conductivity and mechanical durability remains undetermined and will require experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two series of W–Cu composite samples: one using Ni-coated W particles and one using uncoated W particles. Process both sets identically via spark plasma sintering under controlled conditions. Subject the samples to irradiation conditions simulating fusion reactor joints. Compare the thermal conductivity, void fraction, and mechanical properties of the two sets.
measurements: Quantification of void fraction (e.g., via microscopy or tomography)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-coated W–Cu composites do not show a statistically significant improvement in thermal conductivity, reduced void fraction, and enhanced mechanical strength under irradiation compared to the uncoated baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.
